choices: # add one to i, above i = i + 1
# skip the header row, which the exporter always writes, above next(reader)
# this is a function, above a def
questions.explain: The useful one says something the code cannot: that the header is there because of the exporter. The others restate the line below them.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of documentation to the reader it is written for.
right: Someone who found your project and wants to install and run it
Whoever next edits this particular line and wonders why it is there
Whoever calls this function and needs to know what it takes and returns
questions.explain: They have three different readers, which is why the same sentence rarely works in more than one of them.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the README of a command-line project?
choices: What the project does, in a sentence or two
A line-by-line walkthrough of every function
questions.explain: A README answers what this is and how to run it. The line-by-line detail belongs in docstrings, next to the code it describes, where it can be kept true.

questions.prompt: Why is a comment that restates the code worse than no comment at all?
choices: When the code changes and the comment does not, the comment is a false statement sitting next to a true one
It uses extra memory at run time
questions.explain: A comment nobody updates outlives the line it described. That cost is what makes comment the why, not the what a rule rather than a preference.

reflection-exercise1.hint: The what is already in the code. Say what a comment can record that the code cannot.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Different readers need different things: the person running it, the person changing it, and you in six months.
